sections.title: Writing and conventions · required gap check
sections.passage: A community group argues that a school should plant trees near its outdoor learning area. Its claim is narrower than "trees solve every problem": a carefully chosen location may provide shade and support habitat. The group presents a fictional class data table comparing temperatures at a sunny spot and a shaded spot. It also acknowledges counterarguments: planting and watering cost money, and roots or branches may interfere with structures. Its proposal recommends consulting knowledgeable staff, selecting a suitable location, and comparing costs before planting. An effective response to a counterargument does not mock the people who raise it. Instead, it explains how the plan addresses a reasonable concern or why the evidence supports a different choice. The final paragraph asks the school to try a manageable plan and report the results.

sections.title: Writing and conventions · required gap check
sections.passage:
Original drama:
[An apprentice arranges metal type on a table.]
APPRENTICE: If we print the same page many times, will every reader agree with it?
PRINTER: Copies spread words, not agreement.
APPRENTICE: Then accuracy matters before the first copy.
[The printer points to a misplaced letter.]
PRINTER: And readers must question what they read.

Informational companion: In early modern Europe, printing made it possible to reproduce texts more quickly than copying each one by hand. Printed works helped ideas circulate, including religious, scientific, and artistic arguments. Access remained uneven; not everyone could read or obtain books. Greater circulation did not guarantee that every claim was true. Scholars therefore needed observation, reasoning, and the comparison of sources as well as access to texts.

sections.title: Writing and conventions · required gap check
sections.passage:
Original drama:
[An apprentice arranges metal type on a table.]
APPRENTICE: If we print the same page many times, will every reader agree with it?
PRINTER: Copies spread words, not agreement.
APPRENTICE: Then accuracy matters before the first copy.
[The printer points to a misplaced letter.]
PRINTER: And readers must question what they read.

Informational companion: In early modern Europe, printing made it possible to reproduce texts more quickly than copying each one by hand. Printed works helped ideas circulate, including religious, scientific, and artistic arguments. Access remained uneven; not everyone could read or obtain books. Greater circulation did not guarantee that every claim was true. Scholars therefore needed observation, reasoning, and the comparison of sources as well as access to texts.

sections.title: Writing and conventions · required gap check
sections.passage: A student created a portfolio about how travel and communication changed societies. She began with a research question rather than a list of famous people: How did networks connect communities, and whose experiences were left out of the usual accounts? She compared a map, a trade-route reading, and a translated historical account. Her notes separated quotations, paraphrases, and her own interpretations. When two accounts disagreed, she recorded their authors, purposes, and contexts instead of choosing the more dramatic version. The final presentation used a timeline but did not imply that every change happened everywhere at once. It included an argument supported by evidence and a section explaining limitations. The student concluded that a strong portfolio shows not only a polished product but also how the researcher checked and revised the work.
